story_text.value:
Making running somewhat of a routine has the side effect of repeating the same routes very often. As someone raised playing games like Sega Rally or Collin McRae Rally, I found myself thinking of racing against the ghost of a previous run, and that's how the idea for Ghost Runner came to be.

As a semi-retired developer now playing with the new tools of the trade, I put this together (aka iterated with Claude over 12 weeks and about 300 km of runs), and this is what came out.

The biggest challenges were getting the zoom levels and transitions right as you race against up to 6 past versions of you and different performances, as well as the map detail in a way that would work for both road and trail runs.

I'm proud of it and would love for some of you to test it as well and have fun with it.

story_text.value:
Annoyed by slow zip handling in Ruby apps in gems like roo and caxlsx, they use rubyzip underneath which is pure Ruby and does a lot of per entry work in Ruby objects which is slow.

My project keeps the rubyzip API (Zip::File, Zip::InputStream, etc.) but does the parsing compression and file IO in Rust, using the zip crate via magnus/rb-sys. Change a line in your gemfile and I ship precompiled gems so no Rust toolchain to install.

About 6x faster reading lots of small entries, and 2x faster deflating big ones. It also adds a few things rubyzip doesn’t have like limits for zip bombs, an open mode that doesn’t modify the archive, and multithreaded compression.

To check I didn’t break anything, I run rubyzip’s own test suite against it (416 of 476 pass; most of the rest test rubyzip internals), fuzz it against Python’s zipfile, and run the test suites of roo, caxlsx, rubyXL and a few others with ziperu swapped in, working pretty well so far.

I would love to hear ideas for new features, or zip edge cases that annoy you!

title.value: Show HN: Ziperu is rubyzip with a Rust core, same API but faster and safer

story_text.value:
Hi HN!

Suppose you have notes, skills, and agent instructions that are part of your personal workflow, so you do not want them committed to the public repo, but at the same time, you want them to be in the workspace at the correct locations (e.g., AGENTS.md file locations matter), and these files cannot be simply gitignored because you also want versioning for them.

The solution to this is actually just a bit more plain Git.

  $ git status --short                                 # public repo
  ?? AGENTS.md
  ?? notes/

  $ git dupe init                                      # private repo
  Initialized empty Git repository in /home/brian/code/project/.git/dupe/

  $ git dupe add notes/ AGENTS.md                      # private repo
  hint: notes is now hidden from the project's Git; run from the root, 'git dupe unhide -- notes' stops hiding it

  $ git dupe commit -m "Notes and agent instructions"  # private repo
  [main (root-commit) 3eb3af9] Notes and agent instructions
   3 files changed, 3 insertions(+)
   create mode 100644 .gitdupe
   create mode 100644 AGENTS.md
   create mode 100644 notes/todo.md

  $ git status --short                                 # public repo: nothing

  $ git dupe log --oneline                             # private repo: your files
  3eb3af9 Notes and agent instructions
The solution, in short, is versioning those agent files in a repo, say <private-repo> (this repo is private to you and holds the history for your agent files), and that repo shares the same worktree as the public repo <public-repo>. You essentially overlap the two, with <private-repo> put in .git/ (and .git/ is that of the public repo) for a convenient solution.

If you want to read more about the strategy used, there is more comprehensive documentation in the repo.

git-dupe supports macOS, Linux, and Windows and is under the MIT License.

title.value: Show HN: Git-dupe – plain Git per-project private versioning for agent files

story_text.value:
After installing the web extension and clicking its icon it shows a QR code that is scanned by a phone which opens the web app in the browser. When the WebRTC connection has been set up between the devices you can steer a dot on the computer web page by holding a button and pointing the phone. The app also has other presentation clicker features like switching slides, drawing, presenter notes, and can also be used for remote controlling some videos (tested on YouTube and Plex).

Firefox extension: https://addons.mozilla.org/sv-SE/firefox/addon/clikr/ Chrome extension: https://chromewebstore.google.com/detail/clikr/oalndbmcbpchb... Home page: https://www.clikr.app/

I've always been fascinated in how much the web can do. This project started as a fun small POC many years ago when some of these native app-like functions were less common. I got the idea to see if I could make my phone control a "laser dot" on my computer just by tilting the phone like a real laser pointer. Being a web guy I went with web extension + web app. Surprisingly I think I got the basics working in an afternoon or two, having some experience with web extensions from before. Getting the user experience smooth and stable and adding other presentation features in various online tools took more time...

It uses RTCPeerConnection for the communication, Metered as signaling server, and a small protocol for the commands (point, switch slides, etc.). The deviceorientation event is used for getting the orientation (which has to be explicitly allowed on some devices). One issue here is that the angle values don't actually mean anything without a reference. Therefore the first pair of angles received in the extension becomes the origin for that "pointing". The origin on the screen is the middle of the viewport and additional received angles move the dot with those origin values as reference. I.e. it will always start in the middle. This is of course not as good as a real laser pointer but I think it works quite well when you've tried it a bit. Distance to the screen and its size will matter for how much to move the dot which is why there is also a calibration tool.

I like the other features too but I think the laser pointer is the fun one.

There are some paid features (one-time payment, no subscription) but the laser pointer, basic presentation features, and video remote are free and doesn't require an account.

It has some users but it's hard to get them to give feedback so honestly I don't yet know much about how it's performing in real situations. If anyone here tries it out please tell me what you think.

story_text.value:
Hi HN,

I build Valin because my wife needed a way to search across all the saves and all the information she came across online - from recipes, books, children activities, vacation recommendations. She didn't want another AI subscription or another account to manage.

Valin was born - an application that allows users to share to it (almost) any kind of contents from applications (videos, audio, links, papers, reels. etc) and it goes in and using on-device AI transcribes audio, extract key frames of the video, extracts text from the frames and shows Key Takeaways and Summary. This allow users to get an at-a-glance overview of what the save was about and it allows the application to cluster and to find similar saves on the device - to generate new collections or to automatically (if enabled) assign saves to existing collections. And in the end it allows the system to support a chat-like interface where users can quickly get the information they need, not just the save.

I vibe coded it in the last 5 months and I'm pretty happy how it turned out so I wanted to share the TestFlight beta to see if its interesting or useful to other folks.

Features

- fully on-device: no cloud services, no AI subscription, no account needed.

- supports videos, audio, pdf, images

- supports applications: FB, Instagram, Substack, X, Reddit, TikTok, Threads, Voice Memos

- supports iPhone (including Duo) and iPad

- iCloud sync (optional) to allow cross device sync and processing

Limitations:

- it can only work with saves that are available or can be read without a subscription (no logins)

- it only processes in the foreground or background if you approve it when suggested.

Requirements:

- iOS only

- iPhone 15 pro or newer

- iPad with M1 or newer, or the iPad mini with A17 Pro.

Models used:

- Gemma 4 E2B - for summarization, chat and general information extraction

- Embeddings Gemma 300m - for clustering, collection generation and semantic search

- Whisper - for transcribing

What I'm proud of - there are over 10 TLA+ models which I used to model everything from the DAG that processes the saves, to iCloud sync, to GPU/CPU processing of AI requests (since iOS doesn't allow background GPU processing on the iPhones).

It's a beta right now on TestFlight - https://testflight.apple.com/join/gjJQQrqk Would love to hear feedback and suggestions.

Daniel

story_text.value:
Practical Data is a Chrome extension that turns `<table>`s on the web into data visualizations by way of conditional formatting. It makes it easy to see patterns in the data in front of you.

Importantly, it uses a decision model (like Jev) behind the scenes to get around the gotchas normally associated with this, like "green-to-red scale, but high numbers for this column are actually bad", like cost increases, or batter strikeouts, etc.

story_text.value:
Aircad is a professional CAD system running in the browser with deep AI integration. It includes professional grade drafting and documentation tools, NURBS-based solid modeling, and a lot more. You can make professional quality design documents with it. It is all integrated behind a scripting API that can do anything you can do in the interface and also perform complex modeling operations efficiently. It reads and writes file formats like DXF, DWG, STEP, and 3DM.

I built Aircad because I was frustrated with what was out there. Current CAD tools are expensive and slow to improve. New features barely move the needle. With Aircad, you have fast, powerful geometry tools for just about anything, from conceptual models to your final design.

The newer generation of web-based CAD isn’t comprehensive enough to complete a project or is slower than existing desktop products because it sends performance-sensitive work to a server (OnShape), or isn’t designed to scale to real work in a collaborative setting (many "toy" CAD tools).

Current CAD collaboration workflows are fragile, costly, and complex. They’re file-based and separate the design artifacts (eg PDFs) from the source. Collaboration is often an expensive add-on that raises your subscription, is hard to learn, and feels unnatural. Aircad builds it in: version history, drawing comparison, forking, and realtime collaboration.

AI in most CAD tools is tacked on as a plug-in instead of being deeply integrated, and those plug-ins are often inefficient, hard to adopt, and costly. Aircad has a built-in AI agent and a comprehensive scripting API with a stage-and-commit workflow, so you know exactly what is happening during a complex change. You can use AI to write new scripts and commands that extend Aircad with repeatable, shareable workflows.

story_text.value:
hi everyone, i'd like to show my project "Sugo". this project answers a real problem i had:" how can i save tokens if i put a lot of screenshot or PDF's to give to any AI?"

Until recently i was learning to manage RAG system and to run an Ai locally, i got decent result, also with dedicated frameworks. then i realised that the main reason for my bad results was how i managed the files for the RAG.

actualy i work in helpdesk, I'm young and i don't have much experience ;), i immagine you also give Ai's projects, docs and screenshots so a lot of tokens get used. i wondered how the AI converts PDF's and images and wow, it uses a lot, the worst part: the more powerful is the model, the more tokens it use. i'had enough, so i designed Sugo, it use OCR and other tools to convert images, PDFs, documents and presentation into Markdown files, so the Ai understands the content faster.

Right now, in github, there is the 0.1.4 version and includes the lite level (i'm planning a normal level and, for the most demanding, a quality level). if you take a look at the README, it would make me very happy, i had fun designing it.

along the way i came up with the most brilliant name ever. Since i'm italian, the word fit perfectly. "feed your LLM with the sauce, not the water", genius.

For anyone who doesn't know fine italian food the sugo (sauce) is the essential part of a dish, that's where the flavour is, it's what tells you if the plate of pasta is great or a junk, a watery sauce is not great, i want the essence.

Apply this cooking philosophy to IT and you get Sugo.

the best part is that it runs mostly locally, even on a computer with 16 years old hardware (please don't ask, i don't know why i have a computer like that either even though i have one a thousand times better).

One rule i set myself is transparency about my test data, i won't say silly thing like "my product is the best" or "i built it without Ai" i have no reason to hide it. i also won't hide that my account is new (before, i didn't even know hacker news, now i know it's a great place to learn and stay informed). To keep it short, if you look at or try Sugo, feel free to tell me here or on github (i'll try to reply as soon as i can),all the docs, future plans, workflows and info are there.

If something is missing, just ask and thank you for reading all this stuff.

P.S my english is very bad, sorry for any mistakes.
